unactioned_insights.title: Driver heap saturated: running at 98.5% capacity on a streaming job with 58,863 stages
unactioned_insights.description: The driver JVM heap peaked at 1.426 GiB out of 1.447 GiB allocated (98.5% utilisation), and the driver off-heap pool is fully saturated at 100% (1.11 GiB used against 0.375 GiB configured). spark.driver.memory is not explicitly set, leaving the default 1g in effect. This is a Structured Streaming job running 389 micro-batches with an extraordinary ~151 Spark stages per micro-batch (58,863 total stages). The driver accumulates query metadata, StreamingQuery progress objects, WAL state, and stage scheduling overhead in-heap throughout the entire run. With the driver heap this close to exhaustion, any run with a heavier micro-batch — or a slight increase in data volume — risks an OOM on the driver thread, which would fail the entire streaming query silently or force a retry. The time-series data shows the driver heap oscillating between 0.89–1.43 GiB used continuously throughout the 6.5-hour run, confirming sustained pressure, not a transient spike.
unactioned_insights.reason: planner hit its iteration budget before producing recommendations

unactioned_insights.title: Abnormally high stage count for a streaming job (~151 stages per micro-batch) inflating driver overhead
unactioned_insights.description: This Structured Streaming job emits ~151 Spark stages per micro-batch (58,863 stages / 389 batches). A healthy streaming micro-batch typically produces 2–10 stages. The extreme stage fan-out suggests the query plan contains deeply nested transformations, repeated recomputations of un-persisted intermediate results, or per-row Spark actions being triggered inside the streaming foreach/foreachBatch sink. The thread dumps confirm the driver spends all its time inside ProcessingTimeExecutor.execute → MicroBatchExecution.runActivatedStream, and 96.9% of total time is spent in addBatch (12,989s out of 13,422s batch duration). Each additional stage carries driver-side scheduling overhead (DAGScheduler work, metadata retention in WAL) that compounds the heap pressure identified above and sets a hard ceiling on throughput regardless of executor count.
unactioned_insights.reason: planner hit its iteration budget before producing recommendations

unactioned_insights.title: Severely under-utilised compute: vcore utilisation at 14.3% on an always-on, single-worker cluster
unactioned_insights.description: The executor uses only 14.3% of available vcore time (used_vcore_time=13,411s vs vcore_time=94,084s). The time-series confirms vcores_avg_used_over_time=0.10, meaning the cluster idles ~90% of the time. This is a structural mismatch: the job is driver-bound (scheduler overhead from 151 stages/batch) rather than executor-bound, so adding workers would not help — but the cluster is also sized with dynamic allocation disabled and autoscaling off on a persistent single-worker setup. The m7gd.large instance runs on-demand the entire time regardless of workload. The job processes only ~16K source records per micro-batch at 7.6 input rows/sec, yet the cluster runs continuously for 6.5 hours. Historical runs average ~43,200s (12 hours), paying for a full node the entire time.
unactioned_insights.reason: planner hit its iteration budget before producing recommendations

unactioned_insights.title: Current run anomalously short (10th percentile) — not a real improvement, masking chronic SLA risk
unactioned_insights.description: This run completed in 23,521s, which is at the 10th percentile of the 20-run historical baseline (mean=39,552s, std=8,402s, z=-1.91). There were no configuration changes (cluster type, instance type, and worker count have been stable across all 20 runs). The duration distribution shows a bimodal pattern: several runs cluster tightly at ~43,200s (exactly 12 hours) while a few runs land at 16,000–27,000s. The ~43,200s runs are suspiciously round — they suggest the streaming query is being externally terminated (e.g. by a pipeline SLA kill or a scheduled cluster restart) rather than completing naturally. If the normal run time saturates a 12-hour window, the job is chronically failing to finish all available data before being cut off.

agent_insights.identifier: Abnormally high stage count for a streaming job (~151 stages per micro-batch) inflating driver overhead
agent_insights.title: Abnormally high stage count for a streaming job (~151 stages per micro-batch) inflating driver overhead
agent_insights.description: This Structured Streaming job emits ~151 Spark stages per micro-batch (58,863 stages / 389 batches). A healthy streaming micro-batch typically produces 2–10 stages. The extreme stage fan-out suggests the query plan contains deeply nested transformations, repeated recomputations of un-persisted intermediate results, or per-row Spark actions being triggered inside the streaming foreach/foreachBatch sink. The thread dumps confirm the driver spends all its time inside ProcessingTimeExecutor.execute → MicroBatchExecution.runActivatedStream, and 96.9% of total time is spent in addBatch (12,989s out of 13,422s batch duration). Each additional stage carries driver-side scheduling overhead (DAGScheduler work, metadata retention in WAL) that compounds the heap pressure identified above and sets a hard ceiling on throughput regardless of executor count.
agent_insights.evidence: num_spark_stages=58,863; num_spark_jobs=58,834; trigger_count=389 → ~151 stages/batch and ~151 jobs/batch (expected: 2–10); batch_operation_duration.addBatch=12,989s out of total batch_duration=13,422s (96.9%); thread dump shows driver blocked in ProcessingTimeExecutor.waitTillTime between batches; queryPlanning per batch avg=31ms (not the bottleneck — the execution plan itself is the issue); input_records_read=6.2M over 389 batches ≈ 16K records/batch, which is very small — the overhead-to-work ratio is extremely unfavourable.
agent_insights.suggested_action: Inspect the foreachBatch / streaming sink implementation at IngestLander.scala:213. If it issues one Spark action per record or per small group (e.g. individual Delta writes in a loop), consolidate into a single batch write. Persisting intermediate DataFrames that are referenced more than once in the query plan (df.cache() / df.persist()) can also collapse redundant stage chains. Reducing stages per batch to 10–20 would materially cut driver GC, memory pressure, and overall run time.

agent_insights.identifier: Severely under-utilised compute: vcore utilisation at 14.3% on an always-on, single-worker cluster
agent_insights.title: Severely under-utilised compute: vcore utilisation at 14.3% on an always-on, single-worker cluster
agent_insights.description: The executor uses only 14.3% of available vcore time (used_vcore_time=13,411s vs vcore_time=94,084s). The time-series confirms vcores_avg_used_over_time=0.10, meaning the cluster idles ~90% of the time. This is a structural mismatch: the job is driver-bound (scheduler overhead from 151 stages/batch) rather than executor-bound, so adding workers would not help — but the cluster is also sized with dynamic allocation disabled and autoscaling off on a persistent single-worker setup. The m7gd.large instance runs on-demand the entire time regardless of workload. The job processes only ~16K source records per micro-batch at 7.6 input rows/sec, yet the cluster runs continuously for 6.5 hours. Historical runs average ~43,200s (12 hours), paying for a full node the entire time.
agent_insights.evidence: vcore_utilization=0.1425 (14.3%); vcores_avg_used_over_time avg=0.10 across 197 time buckets; vcore_time=94,084s total vs used_vcore_time=13,411s; dynamic_allocation_enabled=false; cluster_autoscaling=false; cluster_workers=1 (fixed); instance=m7gd.large on-demand; mean per-run cost=USD 2.45 across 20 historical runs; input_rows_per_sec=7.6; processed_rows_per_sec=34.
agent_insights.suggested_action: The root cause of low utilisation is the driver-bound stage overhead (see above insight) — fixing that will improve utilisation first. For cost, consider whether this streaming job truly needs a continuous cluster: at only 7.6 input rows/sec from a Kinesis stream, switching to a longer trigger interval (e.g. processingTime='5 minutes' instead of the apparent continuous trigger) would allow fewer, larger micro-batches, drastically reducing stage overhead and potentially enabling a smaller or shared cluster. If a continuous cluster is required, right-sizing the executor to a smaller instance type (the executor uses at most 0.875 GiB heap out of 2.46 GiB allocated) would reduce the on-demand cost without affecting correctness.

triage_result.reasoning:
Insight 0 (driver heap saturated at 98.5%, off_heap_headroom=0.0): The driver heap is nearly exhausted (1.426/1.447 GiB, 98.5%) and the off-heap pool is fully saturated (off_heap_headroom=0.0). Although the executor-side memory_headroom=0.64 is healthy, the driver is the bottleneck here. This is a correctness/stability risk — any heavier micro-batch will OOM the driver, silently failing or retrying the entire streaming query. This maps directly to the "Tight heap headroom" Tier 1 rule (the headroom metric here is driver-side, not executor-side, but the OOM risk is identical in severity). Tier 1.

Insight 1 (abnormally high ~151 stages/micro-batch): This is the root cause of both the driver heap saturation (insight 0) and the chronic SLA overrun (insight 3). 151 stages per micro-batch drives DAGScheduler metadata accumulation in the driver heap and is responsible for the driver CPU time and WAL overhead observed in the time-series. Fixing the query plan (un-persisted intermediate results, per-row Spark actions) would simultaneously reduce driver heap pressure and shrink run duration. Because this is a correctness/structural issue that is the direct root cause of a Tier 1 health problem, it belongs in Tier 1 alongside insight 0.

Insight 2 (severely under-utilised compute, vcore_utilisation=4-14%): The cluster runs a single worker on-demand continuously with dynamic allocation disabled. vcore_utilization is confirmed at ~4% (metrics) / ~14% (enrichment). idle_ratio is essentially 0 only because there is always at least one active task from the streaming trigger, but the actual utilisation is extremely low. This is a classic over-provisioned cluster scenario — reduce the persistent cluster size or move to a smaller instance. Tier 2.

Insight 3 (current run anomalously short, 10th percentile, masking chronic SLA risk): The run at 23,521s is at the 10th percentile (z=-1.91, band=reduced). The bimodal distribution (many runs cluster at ~43,200s = hard 12-hour kill) reveals that the job is routinely cut off before completion. This is fundamentally a duration/SLA observability and alerting concern — not a resource configuration fix. It's a structural monitoring gap that is downstream of the root cause (insight 1, excessive stages per micro-batch). It does not map to a Tier 1 health rule (no retries, no GC crisis, no spill, no OOM), but it does surface chronic unreliability. It's best placed in Tier 4 (fine-tuning / monitoring) as it requires operational changes (SLA window adjustment, alerting, possibly fixing the stage count) rather than a direct config recommendation.

Conflicts: None detected. There is no executor reduction vs. memory reduction conflict (we are recommending driver memory increase, not executor memory change). The skew_ratio=0 and spill is absent, so no conflict rules apply. Insight 2 (reduce cluster size) does not conflict with insight 0/1 (increase driver memory) because they target different resources.

The duration distribution shows a bimodal pattern: several runs cluster tightly at ~43,200s (exactly 12 hours) while a few runs land at 16,000–27,000s. The ~43,200s runs are suspiciously round — they suggest the streaming query is being externally terminated (e.g. by a pipeline SLA kill or a scheduled cluster restart) rather than completing naturally. If the normal run time saturates a 12-hour window, the job is chronically failing to finish all available data before being cut off.
tier4.evidence: task__duration current=23,521s at 10th percentile; baseline mean=39,552s (±8,402s); duration values show clustering at 43,203–43,257s (12.0 hours exactly) in 14 of 20 runs; no config changes across all 20 runs (cluster_max_workers stable, worker_type='m7gd.large' stable); pipeline_sla_value=null but sla metric=415,094s in test_runs; this run's lighter data day (input_rows_per_sec=7.6 vs time-series max=132) explains the short duration.
tier4.suggested_action: Confirm whether the pipeline or cluster has a 12-hour maximum runtime enforced externally (Databricks job timeout, cluster auto-termination). If so, the job is regularly truncated and unprocessed Kinesis records accumulate. The fix requires either reducing per-batch processing time (by addressing the stage-proliferation issue above) so the job processes all records within the window, or switching from a time-limited run to a persistent streaming cluster that is monitored by Kinesis consumer lag rather than wall-clock duration.
